notes: The pinned Greek does not include “Son of God” here. Many manuscripts include that phrase; the title appears explicitly elsewhere in Mark.
The quotation combines language associated with Exodus 23:20, Malachi 3:1, and Isaiah 40:3. Mark introduces it under Isaiah’s name.
“Torn open” uses a verb also used for the sanctuary curtain in 15:38.
The pinned wording says Jesus taught in the synagogue. Some manuscripts also state explicitly that he entered it.
“I came out” can refer to leaving a place or, more broadly, to the purpose of Jesus’ mission. The expression is left open.
The pinned Greek reads “moved to anger.” Many manuscripts read “moved with compassion.” The text does not explicitly identify the object of his anger.
“As a testimony to them” may carry a confirming or challenging force. The recipients are not more precisely identified here.
vocabulary: Greek euangelion: a message of good news.
Greek metanoia: a change of mind or direction, here in response to God.
The forceful verb ekballō is also used in this chapter for driving out demons.
The Greek can also mean tested or put to the test.
Greek paradidōmi: delivered into another’s custody; the wording recurs in Jesus’ arrest and death.
Specialists in written texts and their interpretation, especially the law.
An ancient category of serious skin conditions, not necessarily modern Hansen’s disease.
Cleansing language involves ritual status as well as the bodily condition in this scene.

notes: “At home” can also be rendered “in a house.” The Greek does not identify its owner.
“Their faith” is plural; the text does not single out only the man being carried.
The Greek says “in his house.” Levi is a natural referent in context, but the pronoun can also refer to Jesus.
The pinned Greek ends with “sinners,” without the words “to repentance” found in some manuscripts.
“Wedding guests” renders the expression “sons of the wedding chamber.”
The wording describes making their way while plucking grain. It does not explicitly say they were eating it here.
Mark names Abiathar. The corresponding account in 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech; the translation preserves Mark’s wording.
vocabulary: A portable bed or sleeping pallet.
Jesus’ recurring self-designation, retained without substituting a single interpretation.
A place where taxes or tolls were collected.
Animal-skin containers used for liquids, including wine.
Bread set before God in the sanctuary.
Greek anthrōpos here refers to human beings generally.

notes: The text presents Jesus’ anger and grief together.
The pinned Greek does not include “whom he also named apostles.” Some manuscripts include it.
“Cananaean” represents a term associated with zeal. It does not identify Simon as a Canaanite or establish membership in a later political organization.
The expression rendered “his family” can also mean his associates or those close to him. The subject of “they were saying” is also open to more than one reading.
The warning is explicitly connected to the claim that Jesus has an unclean spirit. The pinned Greek says “eternal sin”; some manuscripts read “eternal judgment.”
Some manuscripts add “and your sisters.” The pinned Greek names his mother and brothers here; verse 35 explicitly includes “sister.”
vocabulary: People associated with or supportive of Herod’s rule.
A name Mark explains as “Sons of Thunder.”
A name used in the accusation about the ruler of demons.
Comparisons or figurative sayings, not only extended stories.
To speak abusively or irreverently against; here directed against the Holy Spirit.
